It looks like a smudge. But the smudge has a shape, and the shape is a dear one, and you press it to your forehead for a moment and go on.

choices.text: Press the margin to your heart

effects.log: A smudge, and a warmth.

choices.text: Copy the smudge exactly

effects.log: The copy keeps the shape and none of the sense.

events.text: You have learned to run a house without a single name in it. The Consort is 'heart'. The children are 'sparks'. The oldest friend is 'the bell', for the way their laugh rings. It sounds like an affectation to outsiders. It is the warmest language heaven has ever heard, and the mortals who pray to your household have begun to borrow it.

choices.text: Teach the mortals your private words

effects.log: The valley takes them up.

choices.text: Keep the words in the house

effects.log: Some languages are for one roof.

events.text: The Court grants you a lasting dispensation: you may sign your edicts with a plain seal and no household names. The first edict you stamp this way is read aloud in the Hall, and a ripple of approval goes round it. A god who gave up the names and kept the love is a thing that heaven finds, to its surprise, to admire.

choices.text: Accept the dispensation graciously

effects.log: The seal is warm in your palm.

choices.text: Decline it and use the old seal anyway

effects.log: The old seal has no names either.

events.text: A very young god of the Laughing River takes your hand at a gathering, turns it over, and says without thinking: 'You have a name in your palm.' Embarrassed, the young god takes it back. 'I do that sometimes. My teacher says it is a knack for what has been taken from a person.' Your palm tingles in a place you did not know it could.

choices.text: Ask what name

effects.log: 'I cannot read it,' says the young god. 'But it is loved.'

choices.text: Thank the young god and let it be

effects.log: The tingle lasts all evening.

events.text: A moth-wing lies pressed in a book from the Court's lending-shelf, and when you lift it, a faint ink-smell rises, and in your chest something large and hollow stirs. You do not know whose book it was. You check the flyleaf: blank. But in the margin of the page, in a small grey hand, are four words: remember to say it.

choices.text: Say it, whatever it is

effects.log: You speak into the empty reading-room. Nobody answers. It feels like being heard.

choices.text: Return the book as it was

effects.log: The librarian nods.

events.text: You wake from a dream of standing in a very quiet library where every shelf is lined with candles, each candle burning for a name, and you are walking down the row blowing out none of them. You wake with a candle's smell in your hair. All morning the dream is a gentle weight on you, like a hand on the shoulder.

choices.text: Light a candle at the temple in the dream's honour

effects.log: It burns steadily.

choices.text: Tell the dream to a priest

effects.log: The priest nods and says nothing, which is exactly right.

events.text: Your Divine Consort comes to the altar at the hour when prayers are fewest and says it plainly: the greater divinity will not open. {sac_name} has stood on the same threshold for centuries, and the faith that feeds {sac_his} domain has thinned to a thread. 'When it breaks,' {sac_he} says, 'I do not become a lesser god. I become a quiet one. Then nothing.'

choices.text: Lay your hand over {sac_his} on the altar

effects.log: The domain-light flickers beneath your palm, warm and low.

choices.text: Say: 'We will find more faith.'

effects.log: {sac_name} smiles at you as one smiles at a tide-table.

events.text: At the Well of Vows where you and {sac_name} swore the oath of the sworn, {sac_he} sits on the rim and drops a single coin of faith into the water. 'I have prayed for a threshold for three hundred years,' {sac_he} says. 'Nothing answers. Worshippers leave, as they do. Tell me you won't pity me.'

choices.text: Say you don't

effects.log: It is nearly true.

choices.text: Offer to share your congregation

effects.log: {sac_name} looks away. 'Don't. I might say yes.'

events.text: {sac_name}, a god of your own lineage, takes you aside at the hearth of the family temple, to which no one has brought an offering in a month. {sac_He} says that the greater divinity is forever out of reach, that faith has ebbed, that the lineage has begun to whisper. 'Do not let them pity me,' {sac_he} says. 'Better they envy a wall than lament a fall.'

choices.text: Promise to say nothing

effects.log: A pledge between kin is the oldest vow.

choices.text: Say the lineage should hear it from {sac_him}

effects.log: {sac_name} considers it. 'Perhaps.'

events.text: {sac_name}, a god you have known since the days of the first temples, tells you at the end of a long evening that {sac_his} faith is ebbing and the greater divinity is shut. {sac_He} speaks calmly, the way a god speaks of weather in a far valley. Then {sac_he} asks how your own congregation fares, and listens to the whole answer.

choices.text: Answer, and say nothing of what you are weighing

effects.log: You are weighing what you could give.

choices.text: Refuse to change the subject

effects.log: 'No. We are speaking of you.' {sac_name} looks relieved.

events.text: {sac_name} returns from a long night of invocation with the domain-light guttering like a candle in a draught, and sets down {sac_his} staff with a hand that shakes. 'Close,' {sac_he} says. 'It was close again.' In the corner, the offering-bowl is empty. It has been empty for a while.

choices.text: Fill the bowl from your own store

effects.log: The bowl glows. It does not last.

choices.text: Sit with {sac_him} in the dark

effects.log: {sac_name} sleeps, the first time in weeks.

events.text: {sac_name} asks you to count the prayers with {sac_him} on the long steps: one for each worshipper still alive in the valleys below. It takes an afternoon and ends in a number that feels like a small town. 'That is who I am responsible to,' {sac_he} says. 'It is not so many. I know their faces.'

choices.text: Count the number twice

effects.log: It does not change.

choices.text: Say it is enough to be a god of a small town

effects.log: {sac_name} wants to believe it.

events.text: You spend a feast of First Fruits at {sac_name}'s side, receiving the few offerings left in {sac_his} temple. A child leaves a boiled egg. An old woman leaves a ribbon. {sac_name} accepts each with a bow so deep it hurts to watch. You learn what it looks like when a god tries to enjoy being needed for the last time.

choices.text: Bow beside {sac_him}

effects.log: The ribbon is tied to your wrist too.

choices.text: Ask {sac_him} what {sac_he} wants of the rest of the age

effects.log: 'To be asked for something,' says {sac_name}.

events.text: {sac_name} wants to walk the border of {sac_his} old domain one more time, and you go. It is a trail of a hundred small shrines in the hills, some tended, most not. {sac_He} kneels at each and says a few quiet words. You carry the water-jar. By the last shrine you are both wet to the knees and neither of you has spoken.

choices.text: Kneel at the last shrine with {sac_him}

effects.log: A small stone god looks back at you.

choices.text: Offer to tend one of the shrines yourself

effects.log: {sac_name} lets you pick.

events.text: {sac_name} asks you to help rewrite {sac_his} hymn, line by line, in the dying light of the evening: a simplified version for mortals who cannot remember the long one. You write, strike out, rewrite. The hymn is plainer now, and sadder, and better. 'Mortals will sing this,' {sac_name} says. 'Even when I am quiet.'

choices.text: Add the last line yourself

effects.log: {sac_name} reads it, and nods.

choices.text: Let {sac_him} have the last line

effects.log: It is a good one.

events.text: The Court's census-gods come at the quarter-day to re-weigh each temple's faith, and {sac_name} stands for the weighing with composure. The scale tips low. A clerk writes a smaller number in the Book of Fates and says, not unkindly, that the rank follows the weight. {sac_name} thanks the clerk. In the corridor {sac_he} leans against a pillar and shuts {sac_his} eyes.

choices.text: Walk {sac_him} home through the cloud-gardens

effects.log: The long way, slowly. {sac_name} does not speak, and does not need to.

choices.text: Ask the clerk to weigh again

effects.log: The clerk refuses with an apology. It was worth trying.

events.text: At the Well of Vows you unweave a share of your domain, thread by thread, and tie the loose ends to {sac_name}'s. The well-water goes bright and then clear. {sac_name} steps back from the rim a larger god than {sac_he} came, and says, in an unsteady voice: 'I can hear the far valleys praying.' You hear only your own breath, smaller than before.

choices.text: Stay at the rim while the new faith settles

effects.log: {sac_name} laughs and weeps at the noise of it.

choices.text: Say nothing about what it cost

effects.log: A good smile, well practised.

events.text: The Court's clerks dispute the transfer for a week. A gift of godhead is not on any form, and the Ledger-God in charge of faith-taxes wants to know whether {sac_name} now owes a levy on your share. You argue with a calm that surprises you. In the end the clerk stamps it GIFT in red, and {sac_name} reads the stamp as if it were a poem.

choices.text: Frame the stamped page

effects.log: It hangs in a small shrine of its own.

choices.text: Pay the clerk's fee and move on

effects.log: Heaven is built on small fees.

events.text: Two shares left your domain, and your altar goes dark for a night. No lamp will light, no incense catch. Mortals come to the door and find it quiet, and leave their offerings in the porch. By dawn the porch is full. They had felt it, somehow, and come to keep watch. You had not known so many knew your name.

choices.text: Light the lamps one by one at dawn

effects.log: Each one catches.

choices.text: Thank the mortals at the door

effects.log: They are embarrassed, and glad.

events.text: A prayer meant for you reaches {sac_name} by mistake in the days after the second share: a farmer begging for a calm harvest-night. {sac_name} answers it, awkwardly, in your style, and sends you a note: 'I find I cannot tell where you end. Was it supposed to be this way?' You write back that you do not know, and that it feels like a gift.

choices.text: Write that the mistake was welcome

effects.log: A warm reply returns within the hour.

choices.text: Offer to teach {sac_him} your old answers

effects.log: The lessons go on for ages.

events.text: The Book of Fates was rewritten in the night. Unmyeong, god of fate, retied a thread in the Court's loom, for reasons no one will give, and {sac_name}'s threshold simply was not there at dawn: it had been moved to the other side of a door that was now open. You hear it from a sleepy scribe. There was nothing for you to give.

choices.text: Visit the loom and thank the knot

effects.log: The loom is quiet, and a little warm.

choices.text: Go to {sac_name} with a plain pot of tea

effects.log: The two of you raise your cups to the fates.

events.text: You were late. By the time you finished the preparations for your gift, a stranger had already offered {sac_name} a share of divinity, quietly, without the Court's blessing, and gone. The threshold stands open. The giver left no name. {sac_name} asks you who it was. You do not know, and for some reason you are glad.

choices.text: Say it was luck

effects.log: {sac_name} accepts the answer, doubtfully.

choices.text: Search for the unnamed giver

effects.log: The search takes a season and ends at a shrine without a statue.

events.text: A cold season passes, and in the spring a long drought breaks over the valleys of {sac_name}'s domain, and the prayers pour in like rain. The threshold needed only a little time and a little faith, and the faith came by itself. You had been planning a gift for ages. You hold it in your hands, now unnecessary, and put it away with something like joy.

choices.text: Join the thanksgiving feast

effects.log: A feast under the dripping eaves.

choices.text: Give the planned gift to a different friend

effects.log: It finds its home.

events.text: A spring in the hills of {sac_name}'s old domain stops running in the autumn, and the villagers say it is because the god has gone quiet. The Court sends a surveyor and a short note. You walk up to the dry basin and sit on its rim. A single drop of water, from nowhere, falls into the dust and is gone.

choices.text: Leave a bowl at the basin

effects.log: It is dry in the morning, but cleaner.

choices.text: Tell the villagers the god is remembered

effects.log: They nod. They will keep a festival there.

events.text: The Court reassigns {sac_name}'s shrine to a young god of a neighbouring domain, with the usual formal courtesy. You attend the handing-over. The new god is bright and eager and has no idea whose house this was. You tell {sac_him}. The new god goes quiet, and asks if the old god's lamps may stay lit.

choices.text: Say yes, and help light them

effects.log: The lamps stay.

choices.text: Say it is the new god's house now

effects.log: The new god looks relieved, and a little ashamed.

events.text: In the valleys below, a festival is held in {sac_name}'s name, as is the mortal custom for a god gone quiet. Children carry paper lanterns shaped like candles. An old woman sings a hymn you wrote together. You stand in the crowd where nobody knows you, and let yourself be one of the faithful for a night.

choices.text: Sing the hymn with them

effects.log: You do not know the words as well as you thought.

choices.text: Light a lantern at the river

effects.log: The current takes it.

events.text: A mortal prays to you for a safe birth, and before you can answer, the prayer is already answered: {sac_name} has heard it first, in a valley that borders yours, and sent a quiet blessing on the same breath. You feel it pass. 'Forgive me,' {sac_name} says later. 'I can hear the whole valley now, and it hurts to be silent when someone is afraid.'

choices.text: Say it is a gift to be answered twice

effects.log: {sac_name} laughs.

choices.text: Ask what else {sac_he} hears

effects.log: Many things. You listen for an hour.

events.text: At the vote on the new Heavenly Court charter, {sac_name} rises in the Council of {sac_realm} and casts the deciding voice in your favour, without a word of speech or explanation. A murmur runs round the hall. Afterwards {sac_he} leaves a single white lotus on the bench where you sat. No note. None is needed.

choices.text: Take the lotus home

effects.log: It never wilts.

choices.text: Cast your own voice for {sac_him} next time

effects.log: A debt of voices, quietly kept.

events.text: On the feast of the dead, {sac_name} comes to your altar and leaves an offering you did not expect: a share of faith, returned, a small glowing bowl of it, as a mortal would leave a bowl of rice. 'A god gives to the gods,' {sac_he} says. 'I give back what I can. It is not a payment. It is an offering.'

choices.text: Accept it as an offering

effects.log: The bowl glows against the altar-stone.

choices.text: Return half of it to the valleys

effects.log: The valleys notice.

events.text: A temple servant sweeping the steps of a shrine you have never visited drops the broom and stares. 'Forgive me,' says the servant. 'You have the walk of someone who once knelt at the Well of Vows with a friend, and gave away more than you had. We keep a statue of that moment in the cellar.' You ask to see it. {sac_past}, it says on the plinth. You know the name.

choices.text: Look at the statue

effects.log: The two faces are strange and familiar.

choices.text: Leave a flower on the plinth

effects.log: You do not know why, and you do.

events.text: In a dream, you stand on a threshold with a lamp, and someone on the far side calls a name you cannot hear. You hold the lamp out and feel it going out of you into a hand that closes round it. You wake with an ache of loss and a feeling of complete rightness. {sac_past}, you murmur, and the room is only the room.

choices.text: Write the dream down

effects.log: The page is full, in a hand you half recognise.

choices.text: Light a lamp for {sac_past}

effects.log: A small flame in the dark.

events.text: The War in Heaven ended at dusk, and now the Unmaking is being read out across the broken stairs: names of the gods of {wo7_foe} struck from the Book of Fates, one by one. In the ruin of a hearth-temple you find a godling, small as a lantern, glowing faintly with a spark that is not quite a domain. The parent's name was on the list. {wo7_name} knows.

choices.text: Shelter {wo7_him} in the dark of the ruin

effects.log: You stand between the child and the reading until it is finished.

choices.text: Wrap {wo7_him} in your own light and call {wo7_him} yours

effects.log: The spark in {wo7_name} brightens against yours, and holds.

choices.text: Bring {wo7_him} to the Heavenly Court's hostage steps

effects.log: The Court gives you a receipt. It is the coldest piece of paper you have ever held.

choices.text: Take {wo7_him} to the white lamp of {wo7_foe}'s kin

effects.log: You carry a white lamp up the broken stair, and the child's spark steadies beside it.

events.text: Among the wreckage of the fallen god's sky-temple, a small voice is reciting a prayer to nobody, a child's prayer, the kind addressed to a parent. It is {wo7_name}, a godling of {wo7_foe}, curled under a toppled altar. The prayer ends. A pause. Then, softly, as an experiment: 'Hello? Are you there?'

choices.text: Answer the prayer in the parent's place

effects.log: You say: 'I am here.' It is not a lie, exactly.

choices.text: Offer to be the one who prays back

effects.log: 'Always,' you say. The child nods.

choices.text: Answer as a representative of the Court

effects.log: The reply is a form. You are not proud of it.

choices.text: Ask the child where the parent's household lies

effects.log: A name comes. Not far.

events.text: The victors are dividing the domains of the fallen. A scribe unrolls a scroll, and you hear a sound from a wine-jar behind the temple storeroom: a hiccup, then a held breath. Inside is a godling of {wo7_foe} with a flicker of something old and dim in the chest, a domain the war has half unmade. The flicker is the only thing the child has left.

choices.text: Seal the jar and say nothing

effects.log: The jar goes into your sleeve. The scribe unrolls another page.

choices.text: Lift {wo7_name} out gently, as your own

effects.log: The flicker brightens in your hands.

choices.text: Present the child to the scribe

effects.log: A tick in a column. A tag. You take it badly.

choices.text: Ask the scribe who the nearest kin is

effects.log: The scribe, startled, looks it up.

events.text: {wo7_keeper}, the hearth-goddess of a mortal village in a far valley, has a small shrine and a smaller offering bowl, and has learned in a thousand years that the Heavenly Court rarely looks at hearths. She looks at {wo7_name}, looks at your sleeve, and says, 'A child by the fire is a child by the fire. It is not for me to say whose.'

choices.text: Leave a gift for the village's harvest

effects.log: The harvest is good that year, and nobody knows why.

choices.text: Promise to visit at the festival of first fires

effects.log: A promise a god makes is heard. Even by hearths.

choices.text: Teach {wo7_name} to keep a small flame

effects.log: The godling's spark learns the shape of an ordinary candle. It is a lesson in humility.

events.text: The mortals of the valley see a new child in the hearth-goddess's care and decide at once she is a niece. They bring millet cakes and wool socks. {wo7_name} has never been fussed over by people who did not know what {wo7_He} was, and spends the first week walking carefully, like a cat in a new house.

choices.text: Let the village fuss

effects.log: They fuss. The godling smiles for the first time.

choices.text: Warn the goddess about the Court's inspectors

effects.log: She nods slowly and begins to practise looking dull.

events.text: The Court's inspectors come through the valley in the third month and ask every hearth if it shelters unregistered godlings. {wo7_keeper} serves them barley tea and speaks for an hour about the weather. In the back room, {wo7_name} sits perfectly still on the sleeping mat with a hand over {wo7_his} own glow.

choices.text: Spend the afternoon distracting the inspectors

effects.log: You are very good at it. They leave with jars of honey.

choices.text: Keep watch from the rafters

effects.log: A bat helps.

events.text: A god's child is entered in the Book of Fates by the scribe of the lower vault. You hold the brush above the line. 'Domain?' asks the scribe, bored. The godling's spark is a half-extinguished thing from a war you won. You write: of the household. The scribe frowns, and writes it down.

choices.text: Write the household as the child's domain

effects.log: The page takes the ink. It is a small domain, but it is a domain.

choices.text: Write nothing and keep the page blank

effects.log: The page is blank. The scribe will ask again.

choices.text: Ask for a minor domain: first small light

effects.log: A modest claim. The scribe pauses over it.

events.text: The first night in your own temple, {wo7_name} refuses a bed, a lamp, and a lullaby, and sits at the foot of your altar, watching the door. You make a pallet of soft prayers and set it beside the godling. 'You need not stay up,' you say. {wo7_name} says: 'I do.' You stay up too.

choices.text: Stay up with {wo7_him}

effects.log: By dawn the godling is asleep against your shoulder.

choices.text: Leave the door open a crack

effects.log: The night comes in. So does the morning.

events.text: At the Lineage banquet an elder god asks pleasantly whose spark is whose, and leans toward {wo7_name} with a kindly, alarming smile. The table goes quiet. The elder knows a war-orphan when he sees one. You set down your cup, and say: 'This is mine. Do not ask where it came from.'

choices.text: Hold the elder's gaze

effects.log: The elder blinks first.

choices.text: Change the subject to the harvests

effects.log: A gift for blandness. The table breathes.

events.text: The hostage steps of the Heavenly Court are long and cold. {wo7_name} sits on the third step in a robe of plain grey, with a clerk at each shoulder, hands folded. Your side calls it a place of safety. The child calls nothing anything. You bring sweets, which are confiscated at the door.

choices.text: Visit every day and be refused

effects.log: On the fortieth day a clerk lets you in.

choices.text: Argue the child's treatment before the Court

effects.log: A formal petition, lengthy, polite. It does some good.

choices.text: Do as told and keep your distance

effects.log: The Court is pleased. You sleep poorly.

events.text: The Heavenly Court wants a sworn custodian for each godling of the beaten pantheon, so that no spark is left unwatched. You are named {wo7_name}'s custodian by a clerk who does not look up. The duty comes with a small stipend of faith, a reporting-day every full moon, and a seal that must be pressed to the child's palm.

choices.text: Press the seal as gently as you can

effects.log: The seal leaves a faint grey mark. {wo7_name} holds out the palm and says nothing.

choices.text: Report on time and keep the reports short

effects.log: Short reports keep the Court bored. Bored is safe.

choices.text: Spend the stipend on the godling's lamp-oil

effects.log: The lamp burns brighter. The Court's accountant raises an eyebrow.

events.text: In the Court's high school for captive sparks, {wo7_name} is placed at a desk with a dozen others from the broken pantheon. The master teaches the hymns of the victors. {wo7_name} learns them perfectly, and sings them in a flat clear voice. After class the godling asks you if it is a lie to sing what you do not mean.

choices.text: Say it is a kind of armour

effects.log: The godling considers this. 'Then I will wear it well.'

choices.text: Say it is a lie, and that sometimes lies keep us alive

effects.log: {wo7_name} nods slowly. It is a hard lesson.

events.text: The road to the border of {wo7_foe} passes through the Plains of Quiet Bells, where every bell is hung with a ribbon for a god unmade. You lead the godling through them under the white lamp. {wo7_name} stops at one bell, and then another, and says softly: 'I think this one was kind.' You cannot tell whether {wo7_He} knows.

choices.text: Wait while {wo7_name} touches each ribbon

effects.log: The bells make no sound. The plain feels listened to.

choices.text: Walk on, gently, to spare {wo7_him}

effects.log: A choice with a cost.

events.text: At the border a council of the fallen house's elders sits under a ragged canopy and will not stand. They look at the godling, and the godling looks at them, and the oldest says: 'We cannot take a child back under a name we no longer hold.' The condition: you must speak for {wo7_name} at their rite of reception, as sponsor, in front of the victors.

choices.text: Agree to sponsor the godling

effects.log: The rite is long. You speak well. The victors are made to listen.

choices.text: Ask the elders to speak for themselves

effects.log: They try. The rite is shorter, and sadder, and holds.

events.text: The Court's Ledger-Gods count sparks nightly by the glow above each temple, and last night yours doubled. A messenger of grey light arrives at dawn and asks whether your sanctuary holds any spark not entered in the Book. The messenger says it as a formality, politely, and keeps one eye on the back rooms.

choices.text: Say the extra spark is a friend's, passing through

effects.log: The messenger notes it, and does not believe it.

choices.text: Present the godling and ask for a charter

effects.log: A formal request. It begins the Court's long process of saying no.

events.text: Your own patron, the Lady of the Long Tide, summons you in a sea-cave and does not offer a seat. She says she has been told you shelter a godling whose parent the Court unmade. She says it flatly, like a tide-table. 'I do not forbid it. I only observe that the Court will notice, and when it does, I will not be standing in front of you.'

choices.text: Say you will stand without her

effects.log: The tide goes out as you say it. She nods slowly.

choices.text: Say the child can be placed elsewhere

effects.log: She is not surprised. She is not pleased either.

events.text: A rumour at a dawn-market, among the faith-sellers, passes from stall to stall: that a certain sanctuary has a fire that burns where no god sits. By noon three pilgrims have asked to see it. By dusk a pair of wardens from the Court of Vows are asking too. The stalls close early, all at once, as if on a signal.

choices.text: Lie to the wardens and bar the door

effects.log: The door holds for the night.

choices.text: Open the door and hand over the record

effects.log: A paper, a name, a tag.

events.text: A grey-robed envoy of the fallen pantheon sits in your outer court at the hour of lamps, with a staff and a small drum. He says he has come only to ask, in the old courtesy, whether any fallen spark has found shelter here. He taps the drum once, softly, in a way that is also a question to anyone who knows how to hear it.

choices.text: Answer the drum with a single tap

effects.log: He bows to the ground. The spark may go home.

choices.text: Say there is no such spark

effects.log: He taps again, once. Then he goes. He will return.

events.text: A lamp-lighter of the old house appears at your threshold, a plain mortal-seeming woman with a ladder, and tells you she has lit the lamps of a hundred temples looking for one particular glow. She says she is not asking for the child. She is only asking whether a lamp in your window has a small warm flame at its centre. It has.

choices.text: Light the lamp brighter and say nothing

effects.log: She looks at the flame, and nods, and goes.

choices.text: Draw the curtain

effects.log: The lamp-lighter looks at the curtain a long time.

events.text: The oldest of the fallen house's ancestors, a faded thing of ash and dust, drifts up to your altar in the night and settles on the offering-bowl. It cannot speak, but it can ask: it turns toward the godling's door and waits, with a patience that has outlasted its own unmaking.

choices.text: Open the godling's door

effects.log: A long hush. The ancestor and the child regard each other.

choices.text: Close the door and bank the fire

effects.log: The ash drifts away. You will think of it for ages.

events.text: {wo7_name} is old enough to receive a first prayer: a mortal farmer asks, on the edge of a field, for rain. The godling's domain is not rain. It is something nearly gone, a small old thing about the last warmth of embers. Still {wo7_He} listens as if the farmer's whole life were in the prayer, and answers the best way {wo7_He} can.

choices.text: Show {wo7_him} how to answer with warmth

effects.log: The farmer feels a faint comfort in the cold dawn and plants anyway.

choices.text: Show {wo7_him} how to pass the prayer on to a rain-god

effects.log: A good lesson in humility.

choices.text: Say nothing and watch

effects.log: {wo7_name} learns the harder way.

events.text: The godling's spark gutters in the autumn when no one offers anything to it, and {wo7_He} sits at the altar, dimmer by the day. You realise what the war really took: not a parent, but a congregation. A domain needs faith the way a fire needs air. You fetch every mortal in the valley to the shrine on the feast of first fires.

choices.text: Ask the villagers to leave one small offering

effects.log: By dusk, the spark burns brighter.

choices.text: Tell them the story of the fallen god

effects.log: Mortals love a story. The spark takes hold.

events.text: {wo7_name} asks what a god is for. The question is old and plain. You say a god is for those who pray, and the godling says, 'But who do I pray to?' It is the first time you have realised {wo7_He} has never had anyone to pray to. You show {wo7_him} how it is done, and then step aside and let {wo7_him} choose a name.

choices.text: Let {wo7_him} choose without hints

effects.log: The name {wo7_He} chooses is no one you know. It is just right.

choices.text: Offer yourself as an option

effects.log: {wo7_name} considers this, and accepts, with a nod.

events.text: In the spring, mortals begin to carve a small grey moth into the lintel of the valley's houses and no one can say why. The godling watches the carvers from the temple roof, bewildered and shy. 'Do they know?' {wo7_He} asks. 'No,' you say. 'They just feel it.'

choices.text: Say the domain is returning by itself

effects.log: {wo7_name} glows a little.

choices.text: Say it is the village's own doing

effects.log: Which is also true.

events.text: A page of the Book of Fates comes loose at the lower vault and floats down to the valley on a draught, and lands on {wo7_name}'s lap. The godling reads it. It is the Unmaking roll of the fallen house, with a name underlined by a clerk's careless thumb. {wo7_He} looks up, white as the page. 'Is this who I think it is?'

choices.text: Tell the truth, gently, with your hand on the page

effects.log: {wo7_name} nods, and does not weep. Not yet.

choices.text: Take the page away and say you will explain tomorrow

effects.log: Tomorrow is a coward's word. {wo7_name} waits.

choices.text: Say the page is a forgery

effects.log: The godling does not believe it, and neither of you says so.

events.text: You are summoned to the shrine at midnight by a ring of the little bell, and find {wo7_name} sitting on the altar steps with a candle. 'I know whose I am,' {wo7_He} says. 'I knew from the first night. I only wanted to see whether you would say it to me.' The candle gutters. You say it.

choices.text: Tell it, all of it, from the war

effects.log: It takes a long time. {wo7_name} listens, and when you finish, hands you the candle.

choices.text: Say you were waiting for {wo7_him} to ask

effects.log: It is partly true. {wo7_name} smiles faintly.

events.text: The truth reaches {wo7_name} from a mortal prophet in the market square, who sings it, badly, for coins. The godling listens to the whole song. Then {wo7_He} returns to the temple, lights every lamp, and sits before the altar until you come. 'I heard it,' {wo7_He} says. 'Is it true that you could have walked away?'

choices.text: Say yes, and that you did not

effects.log: It is all you have. {wo7_name} takes it.

choices.text: Say you do not remember deciding

effects.log: A truth of its own.

choices.text: Ask what {wo7_He} would have wanted

effects.log: 'This,' says the godling.

events.text: On the festival of Unmaking, the godling asks to be allowed to light the first candle for the gods of {wo7_foe}, and asks you to hold the taper. 'I do not forgive the war,' {wo7_He} says, steadily. 'I only know who held the candle.' Behind you, the mortals of the valley come with their own, one by one, and the lamp-field fills.

choices.text: Hold the taper for as long as it takes

effects.log: The field of lamps is a small, bright sea.

choices.text: Add your own light to the field

effects.log: Your flame joins the others.

events.text: A mortal child of the valley, playing in the temple stores, finds an old tablet of the war: a victory list, with the seal of your lineage. The child reads it aloud, laughing, to the godling. It is a list of the unmade, and one name on it is {wo7_name}'s parent. The laughter stops. The tablet falls with a crack on the floor of the shrine.

choices.text: Say you did not carve the list

effects.log: Nobody says anything. The tablet lies in two pieces.

choices.text: Kneel and pick up the pieces

effects.log: A sad gesture. {wo7_name} walks out.

choices.text: Let {wo7_him} go to the dark

effects.log: The door shuts.

events.text: You told {wo7_name} the truth before anyone else could, and the godling heard it standing, without a word. Then {wo7_He} asked for one night. In the morning the offering-bowl is empty, the ember gone, and a single grey moth has been pinned to the lintel. It is not a farewell. It is a notice.

choices.text: Take down the moth and keep it

effects.log: You keep the moth in a locket.

choices.text: Leave it on the lintel

effects.log: It watches the door for ages.

events.text: In an old hymnal in the valley's roadside shrine, a mortal priest finds a verse in an unknown tongue and sings it for the godling, who recognises it at once. It is the dying domain's own liturgy, hidden in mortal song for ages by a god who knew the war was coming. {wo7_name} learns it in a week and sings it back, and the whole valley hums.

choices.text: Sing it with {wo7_him}

effects.log: The liturgy takes hold. A small domain stirs.

choices.text: Copy it into the Book of Fates

effects.log: Heaven learns a hymn it forgot.

events.text: {wo7_name} builds a loom in the temple loft and weaves, thread by thread, a banner of the fallen house, from memory and from rumour. When it is hung, it shows a pattern none of the scribes can name. 'It is the shape of the domain,' says {wo7_name}. 'It is not mine to keep.' The banner is hung in the Court's long hall.

choices.text: Stand beside the banner at its unveiling

effects.log: The hall falls quiet.

choices.text: Let the godling stand alone

effects.log: {wo7_name} does. It is {wo7_his} day.

events.text: The grown godling comes before the Court of Vows with a writ in hand and asks to be heard against you. The charge is read: that you took a spark from its house and its fate. The gods of the Court turn toward you, lazily. {wo7_name} stands very straight in the dock of light, and says: 'I want it judged.'

choices.text: Defend yourself before the Court

ok.log: Your plain account lands. {wo7_name} lowers the writ.

fail.log: The Court hears you coldly. The writ stays standing.

choices.text: Concede the charge and ask for mercy for the child

effects.log: The Court is surprised. {wo7_name} is moved.

choices.text: Ask to speak with {wo7_him} in private first

effects.log: The Court allows it. A room, a lamp, two chairs.

events.text: At the foot of the old temple a grown god of the fallen house holds a spear of dusk and asks, quietly, whether you will meet {wo7_him} on the steps, in the old way, with no one watching. The old way is a duel of domains. It is not meant to kill. It is meant to be understood.

choices.text: Meet {wo7_him} in the old way

ok.log: The duel ends without a mark. {wo7_name} bows, and the steps are quiet.

fail.log: You are outmatched, and {wo7_name} stops the duel before it harms you.

choices.text: Refuse the duel and offer your hands empty

effects.log: {wo7_name} lowers the spear a long moment.

choices.text: Offer to talk before any duel

effects.log: The spear is grounded. The talk begins.

events.text: A message arrives on the smoke of a hundred censers: the grown godling will be at the Well of Listening at the turn of the tide, and invites you, alone, to answer for the night of the Unmaking. The Well hears all truths said into it. You go. {wo7_name} stands at the rim with the stars behind. 'Say it to the Well,' {wo7_He} says.

choices.text: Say the whole truth into the Well

ok.log: The Well gives your words back whole. {wo7_name} bows to the water.

fail.log: Your voice shakes, and the Well gives back only the shaking.

choices.text: Tell {wo7_him} the story, not the Well

effects.log: A story, told eye to eye.

choices.text: Stay silent and lower your head

effects.log: The Well says nothing either.

events.text: A lamp stands in the window of the old temple, and in the window of the valley hearth, and in yours. {wo7_name} walks from one to the other on the night of first fires and relights each in turn. When the three flames are steady, the godling says only: 'There. Now we are a household.'

choices.text: Sit by the three lamps

effects.log: They burn all night.

choices.text: Say the name of the household aloud

effects.log: A name nobody has said in ages.

events.text: The Court assigns {wo7_name} and you joint charge of a small shrine at the edge of the Plains of Quiet Bells, to be kept by one of the fallen house and one of the victors. It is meant as a punishment for both. The two of you keep it for ages and, to the Court's mild annoyance, keep it well.

choices.text: Ring a bell for the fallen

effects.log: It sounds for the first time in ages.

choices.text: Serve tea to the pilgrims

effects.log: Both houses come.

events.text: {wo7_name} left the valley on the first day of spring with a bundle and a grey moth on the shoulder, and the hearth-goddess watched from her door until the road bent. She told you a week later that the godling had left a thing behind: a single unlit candle on the sill, and a note saying only: not yet.

choices.text: Leave the candle where it is

effects.log: It stays there, patient and unlit, for ages.

choices.text: Light it, and say a prayer

effects.log: It burns for a day. Somewhere, perhaps, it is seen.

events.text: A wandering priest passes through the valley and mentions, over bread, a young god who keeps a shrine of embers on the Plains of Quiet Bells and offers any traveller a warm place and no questions. The priest cannot say the god's name. You do not ask. You send a basket of kindling, unlabelled, with the next caravan.

choices.text: Add a line with the kindling

effects.log: 'Whenever you wish.'

choices.text: Let the kindling speak for you

effects.log: A basket of dry wood is a very old kind of letter.

events.text: The godling comes to your temple on the feast of its own naming and lays a garland on your altar, which is not done for a living god. 'It is the custom of my house,' {wo7_He} says. 'We garland those who kept the fire.' The altar-flame leans toward the garland as if to read it.

choices.text: Accept the garland with both hands

effects.log: The flame settles.

choices.text: Tie half of it to the godling's door

effects.log: A shared gift is a double gift.

events.text: The Court has made {wo7_name} a Keeper of the lower vault, with a seat, a quill and the right to speak. The godling's first act is to correct a clerk's error in a roll of the unmade, quietly, with a steady hand. You read the correction in the morning. It is your name, in the margin, restored to a line it was left off.

choices.text: Send a prayer of thanks

effects.log: A short one.

choices.text: Say nothing and keep the page

effects.log: You keep the page for ages.

events.text: The lamp over the old house is lit, and the fallen house is a house again, small, quiet, and full of children's footsteps. The elders send word that the godling is well. A smoke-borne gift arrives with the word: a flask of the dusk-oil used in their rites, with a stopper carved in the shape of a moth.

choices.text: Burn a drop of it at your altar

effects.log: The flame turns violet, then gold.

choices.text: Keep the flask sealed

effects.log: A promise unspent.

events.text: The mortal valley no longer counts the years, but the hearth-goddess does. {wo7_name} is now a young god with a grey moth on the lintel and a bowl of embers, still nameless in any Book, still known to every grandmother of the valley as the godling at the corner shrine. The Court has never come back. You think it has forgotten.

choices.text: Let it forget

effects.log: Better a small peace than a great fame.

choices.text: Visit on the feast of first fires

effects.log: A warm cup, a warmer room.

events.text: You are shown round a shrine in a mortal valley by a hearth-goddess who has never met you and who, halfway through the tour, stops talking and stares. 'You have been here before,' she says. 'You came with a little spark in your coat. I would know that stoop anywhere.' You have never been. But you know the place by smell.

choices.text: Ask her to describe the spark

effects.log: She does, in loving detail. Your throat tightens.

choices.text: Say you are only passing through

effects.log: She nods, and hands you a cup of millet tea.

events.text: A grey moth lands on your sleeve at the door of the Heavenly Court and will not go. You have never seen one like it, and yet your hand rises to cup it as if you had done so a thousand times. The moth leaves a faint, sweet scent of embers. You find you are crying, and a clerk, passing, hands you a handkerchief without asking.

choices.text: Carry the moth outside and release it

effects.log: It circles your head once and goes.

choices.text: Keep the moth until it leaves of its own will

effects.log: It does, at dusk.

events.text: The border-god of {wo7_foe} will take the godling back on one condition: the Court of Vows must witness that no victor's hand rests on the child. You stand beside the child before the Court's bored witnesses, and a clerk asks whether there is any claim upon the spark. You say there is none. It is the truest thing you have said all age.

choices.text: Say it clearly and step aside

effects.log: The clerk writes it down. The border-god bows.

choices.text: Add that the child goes freely

effects.log: The words are not required. They are kind.

events.text: A woman in a black shawl stopped you at the well last week and asked, with a smile, for a cup of water. This morning the people you love are around the breakfast table, and where their names should be there is a smooth, cold place, like a hearthstone after the fire has died. On the doorstep lies a single pinch of grey ash, in the shape of a hand.

choices.text: Sweep the ash up carefully

effects.log: It is cold as winter ground. A weary witch is somewhere, collecting names.

choices.text: Sit down to breakfast and say nothing

effects.log: You pass the bread. You do not say the names. Nobody notices yet.

events.text: At the autumn fair you bought a battered almanac from a pedlar who would not look you in the face, and read it all night: the planting dates, the moon tables, the long forbidden appendix at the back. In the morning, the people at your table are strangers with kind faces. The last page of the almanac has a blank space where a line was, and the ink on your fingertips is black.

choices.text: Throw the almanac in the fire

effects.log: It falls out again. Singed, whole, and cold. That is the first clue.

choices.text: Write a label for each face

effects.log: You make a list of faces and write someone I love beside each.

events.text: After weeks of a hard training, your qi turned sour in the night, running up the wrong channels with a fever that left you wringing wet. By morning the fever has broken, your body is strong, your hands are steady, and the names of the people you love are gone. They stand around the bed in worried silence. You know every face, and not a single word for any of them.

choices.text: Return to your sleeping-mat and feel for the damage

effects.log: There is a cold place in the chest, with a warm place beside it.

choices.text: Go out and work the fields beside them anyway

effects.log: A name is not a field. Work is work.

events.text: The one you married has begun tying coloured strings to things around the house: red on the water bucket, blue on the door-latch, green on the pillow. Each is, you realise, a way of saying a thing to you without a word. You touch them as you pass, one by one. 'I know you,' says someone from the doorway, kindly. 'That's enough for now.'

choices.text: Tie a string of your own to the bucket

effects.log: A yellow one. It stays there for years.

choices.text: Hold the strings against your chest

effects.log: They are rough and warm.

events.text: The market is full of children playing a game where each calls the others by a made-up name, and the children of the house join in with a shout. One of them looks up and asks what you would like to be called today. It is a game, but there is something real inside it. You choose a name from the sky: Heron. Your children whoop, and the name sticks for a season.

choices.text: Be Heron for the whole day

effects.log: The children carry the name home like a trophy.

choices.text: Say you'd rather be called Parent

effects.log: They laugh, and it stays on, gently.

events.text: A neighbour sends a basket of eggs over the fence, with a note: from your friend across the lane. You cannot say the friend's name. You write a thank-you that begins 'Dear friend' and send it back with half the eggs. The reply comes by the same small boy: 'You always did that. I do not mind.' You hold the note a long time.

choices.text: Send the boy a copper for his trouble

effects.log: The boy is delighted.

choices.text: Resolve to find the cause

effects.log: The resolve is firmer than usual.

events.text: The ferry-woman, who knows everything that crosses her river, says there is a hedge-sorceress who lives past the last bridge, in a hut with ash-coloured thatch. They call her the Ash Widow, because every husband she had burned to a name on a gravestone. 'She takes what you give her,' says the ferry-woman. 'Never offer her your own name.'

choices.text: Ask what she takes besides names

effects.log: 'Whatever you can spare,' says the ferry-woman.

choices.text: Pay the ferry-woman for the crossing

effects.log: The fare is a few coppers. The warning was free.

events.text: The Ash Widow's hut stands at the end of a track of black stones, and when you knock, the door opens by itself. Inside, a hundred small jars stand on shelves, each stoppered with grey wax, each with a thread of smoke curling in the bottom. A voice from the back room, dry as husks, says: 'Come in, come in. Mind the jars.'

choices.text: Look at the nearest jar

effects.log: A thread of smoke, shaped like a word.

choices.text: Say you have come about a name

effects.log: The voice laughs. 'They all have.'

events.text: The Ash Widow sits in a rocking chair with a jar in each hand and her shawl pulled round her shoulders. 'I do not give them back for silver,' she says. 'I give them back for a bargain. I am old, and lonely, and sick of the smell of my own smoke. Sit with me for a season. Cut my wood. Talk to me. Then we will see about your names.'

choices.text: Agree to the season

effects.log: She nods, satisfied. 'Good. The wood-pile is round the back.'

choices.text: Offer a story and a loaf instead

effects.log: She sniffs, and takes both.

events.text: The schoolmaster in the next village keeps a shelf of banned books and, when you ask him about the almanac, goes pale. 'There were three printings,' he says. 'The first was burned. The second was lost. The third was sold to a pedlar, who sold it on. Every reader forgot something. I have never seen a reader forget so much, and live.' He offers you tea.

choices.text: Ask how the first reader was cured

effects.log: 'He wasn't,' says the schoolmaster. 'But he left notes.'

choices.text: Ask for the notes

effects.log: He sighs, and fetches them.

events.text: The first reader's notes are in a shaky hand on the back of tax receipts. They say: names do not leave, they hide in the places they were last said. The writer lists a bench, a gate, an orchard, a fishing-post. He ends: 'I found the bench and nothing more. Perhaps you will find the rest.' You pack a lunch and go looking for benches.

choices.text: Start with the bench closest to your door

effects.log: A weathered plank under an old pear tree.

choices.text: Make a map of all the places on the list

effects.log: A day of walking. A satisfying, useless map.

events.text: At the pear-tree bench you sit with the notes in your lap and say, aloud, what you remember: the shape of a laugh, the weight of a head on a shoulder, the sound of a name you cannot say. A single pear drops from the branch into your lap. It is warm. It smells of something you almost know, and almost have a word for.

choices.text: Eat the pear

effects.log: It tastes of someone's smile. You do not know whose.

choices.text: Press it in the notes

effects.log: The page beneath it is blank, and somehow right.

events.text: The bone-setter at the market, who has seen every kind of fever, tells you the sour qi is common, and the loss of names is rare, and that the two sometimes go together. 'It scars the memory,' he says, rubbing his thumbs. 'But scars can be followed back. You must go and sit very still, in the place where it began, and feel for the warm spot.'

choices.text: Ask where the warm spot is

effects.log: 'Wherever you feel most at home,' he says.

choices.text: Ask how long it takes

effects.log: 'As long as it takes,' he says, cheerfully.

events.text: In your own sleeping-room at dusk you sit on the mat where the fever turned and feel for the scar. There is a cool place and a warm place. You put your palm on the warm one. A name tries to rise and sinks again. A smell of woodsmoke. A sound of someone laughing in the next room, which turns out, when you open your eyes, to be a neighbour.

choices.text: Stay longer and breathe slowly

effects.log: The warmth grows. It has the shape of a name, nearly.

choices.text: Mark the mat with a thread

effects.log: A thread of red wool.

events.text: The bone-setter teaches you the Seven Breaths: seven slow breaths for each name, a pause between that is the length of a held heart. The first three come easily. At the fourth, you feel something shift, deep and faint, like a stone settling in a river bed. The bone-setter, watching, says nothing, but nods.

choices.text: Finish all seven

effects.log: It takes the whole evening. At the end your cheeks are wet.

choices.text: Rest and try again tomorrow

effects.log: Rest helps. Sleep is full of faces.

events.text: A season goes by chasing a woman who is said to cure names, and who turns out to be a hat-seller with a good line in patter. She laughs when you explain, kindly, and sells you a hat. It is a nice hat. It does not cure anything. You wear it home anyway, past the pear tree, and some of the children laugh.

choices.text: Wear the hat to the fair

effects.log: It earns you a free bowl of noodles.

choices.text: Give the hat to a child

effects.log: The child is delighted.

events.text: You wait at the crossroads shrine for three market days for a travelling healer who is rumoured to know the answer. He never comes. The crossroads god, a modest little appointed thing with a carved post, accepts your offerings of rice and says nothing at all. When you finally leave, you do it without bitterness.

choices.text: Leave a bowl of rice at the shrine

effects.log: In case the healer comes late.

choices.text: Walk home the long way

effects.log: It takes a day. You see the valley properly.

events.text: On the last night of the season, the Ash Widow rocks in her chair a long time and then rises and goes along the shelves, uncorking jars one by one. Out come the threads of smoke, drifting toward you, and every one ends in your chest like a bell. When she reaches the end of the shelf, she sets down the last jar and says, tired: 'There. You've paid enough.' You say each name, softly, one by one.

choices.text: Say every name aloud, at the door

effects.log: She hears them from her chair.

choices.text: Leave her the wood you cut

effects.log: She never mentions it. The wood-pile is the neatest in the valley.

events.text: The last name returns in the pear orchard on a day of light rain. You are sitting on the bench with the first reader's notes in your lap and the blossoms coming down, and something small and bright slides back into the place it belongs, like a coin falling into a bowl. You say the name aloud. It is the best sound you have ever made.

choices.text: Go and find them at once

effects.log: You run.

choices.text: Sit a while and let it settle

effects.log: The name is yours. It stays.

events.text: On the seventh night of the seventh breath, the long unfolding comes: a warmth that opens in the chest and runs out to your fingers, and the rooms of memory light up one by one, each with a name in a hand you know. You walk down the line of them, reading, and by the end you are crying and laughing in the dark of your own house.

choices.text: Wake the household and say their names

effects.log: They come at once, bleary and glad.

choices.text: Sit in the dark and say them to yourself

effects.log: The names are yours. They stay.

events.text: A bitter herb tea recommended by the bone-setter makes you violently ill for two days, and you lie in the dark with a basin by the bed and a neighbour pressing damp cloths to your forehead. 'Too strong,' says the bone-setter, apologetic, when he looks in. 'My mistake.' You do not blame him. You do not get your names back either.

choices.text: Rest, as told

effects.log: You rest.

choices.text: Ask for a gentler remedy

effects.log: He says there is one, and he will write it out.

events.text: It happens at the ferry, in the dull middle of a grey afternoon: the ferry-woman calls a name across the water, a passenger's name, and it falls into you whole. You say it aloud before you can stop. '{nc_name},' you say. Across the planks, the one you said it to turns and looks at you, and does not move. 'Say it again.'

choices.text: Say it again, and again

effects.log: {nc_name}. {nc_name}. The ferry rocks gently.

choices.text: Take their hands and say nothing more

effects.log: Their hands are warm. You do not need to say it twice.

events.text: The elderly woman who sells pickled radishes at the corner stall looks up when you pass and says, 'Oh, you again,' though you have never bought a radish from her. Then, embarrassed: 'Forgive me. You have the face of someone who once spent all day trying to say a name to me and could not.' She looks away, and you find you want to cry.

choices.text: Ask who it was

effects.log: 'I never knew,' she says. 'I just remember it was raining.'

choices.text: Buy a jar of radishes and go

effects.log: They taste like home.

events.text: At a harvest fair a puppeteer's story ends with a woman sitting alone at a table laid for two, saying a name to the empty chair, and the empty chair answering. The audience claps. You do not. You sit with your hands in your lap, and a feeling in your chest like a held breath. The puppeteer, packing up, glances your way and quietly bows.

choices.text: Bow back

effects.log: The puppeteer smiles.

choices.text: Ask which story it was

effects.log: 'Old,' says the puppeteer. 'Every village has it.'

events.text: The Ash Widow's season ends in a quarrel over a pot of stew, and she bangs the door in your face, and no jar is opened. On the road home in the rain you hear her cackle through the window, or perhaps a crow. You curse, and then you laugh, and then you walk on with wet boots, a little lighter and no less empty.

choices.text: Come back in spring with a better stew

effects.log: It might work. It might not.

choices.text: Walk on and think of a new road

effects.log: The rain does the rest of the thinking.

events.text: A child at the fair holds up a painted wooden duck and shouts a name at the top of its lungs, to a friend across the stalls. The name goes through you like a pin. It is not yours, and it is, and by the time the child has run off with the duck you are saying it softly to yourself in the crowd. '{nc_name}.' You say it again, and again, and a woman beside you says, 'Do you want to sit down?'

choices.text: Sit down and say it again

effects.log: {nc_name}. The woman fetches you water.

choices.text: Go and find {nc_name} at once

effects.log: Through the stalls, past the ducks, down the lane.

events.text: The graveyard is the one place where you do not miss the names, because there they are all in stone, and all unreadable to you. You walk the rows on the feast of the dead and put a pinch of rice on each. The gravedigger, an old man with a limp, says it is a good habit. You say you have no choice. He says that is how habits start.

choices.text: Leave rice at every grave

effects.log: A long afternoon.

choices.text: Ask the gravedigger to read the stones aloud

effects.log: He does. You do not hold on to the names. You hold on to the voice.

events.text: The village has made a small custom of your trouble, as villages will. When you come into the inn, the landlord says 'the usual, friend,' and the regulars lift their cups in your direction and say friend. It is not a name. It is, you realise, better than a name: it is what everyone calls everyone who is loved, and you are loved by everyone in the room.

choices.text: Raise a cup to the room

effects.log: The room cheers.

choices.text: Buy a round for the house

effects.log: A cheerful sum, well spent.

events.text: {sac_name}, the one you married, comes in from the terraces at dusk with the rice-hat in hand and says it, quite simply, over the supper bowls: the last gate of this small heaven will not open. Not for lack of trying. {sac_He} has climbed the mountain path nine times, and each time the sky has sat on {sac_his} shoulders like a lid. 'There is nothing above this,' {sac_he} says. 'And my years are running down.'

choices.text: Set down your bowl and hold {sac_his} hand

effects.log: The lamp gutters. Neither of you eats.

choices.text: Say: 'We will look for another way up.'

effects.log: {sac_name} smiles at you as one smiles at a good child.

events.text: On the ferry-landing where you and {sac_name} swore to be brother and sister of the road, {sac_he} sits with feet over the water and tells you the truth: {sac_he} stands at the top of what a cultivator of this small world can reach, and the sky above is the end of the world. 'The Maker did not leave room above me,' {sac_he} says, half joking. 'I have looked.'

choices.text: Sit on the planks beside {sac_him}

effects.log: The river carries the evening past.

choices.text: Ask how many years are left

effects.log: 'Fewer than I like,' says {sac_name}.

events.text: {sac_name} is your own blood, an elder cousin who taught you your first form in the orchard, and has been the strongest cultivator in the district since you were small. Today {sac_he} meets you at the well and says that the strength has stopped growing, that the old path ends at a ceiling, and that the years of a body do not wait. 'Don't tell the family,' {sac_he} says.

choices.text: Promise to keep it quiet

effects.log: The oldest vow there is, between kin.

choices.text: Say the family should know

effects.log: {sac_name} looks stung, then relieved.

events.text: {sac_name}, who you have shared a road and a supper with for twenty years, tells you at the end of a market day that the high gate of this world will not move for {sac_him}, and that {sac_his} years are running down, one by one, like beads on a string. {sac_He} says it as one mentions bad weather. Then {sac_he} asks how your cabbages are doing.

choices.text: Answer about the cabbages, and keep the secret

effects.log: Inside, you are already counting what you could give.

choices.text: Refuse to change the subject

effects.log: 'No. We are talking about this.' {sac_name} looks relieved.

events.text: {sac_name} comes down from a long retreat on the high ledge with grey in the beard and a cough that was not there in spring. 'Close,' {sac_he} says. 'It is always close.' You press a warm bowl of broth into {sac_his} hands. The hands shake a little around it.

choices.text: Pay the apothecary for the strong tonic

effects.log: The tonic helps the body. It does not help the gate.

choices.text: Sit with {sac_him} through the night

effects.log: {sac_name} sleeps for the first time in weeks.

events.text: The children of the village are being taught the school's first form in the courtyard, and {sac_name} watches from the bench, smiling at the clumsiest. Afterwards, at the pump, you hear {sac_him} say very quietly that {sac_he} will never teach that form to a child of {sac_his} own. {sac_He} drinks from the pump and wipes {sac_his} face with a sleeve.

choices.text: Say nothing, and pump for {sac_him}

effects.log: The water is cold and good.

choices.text: Say that {sac_he} teaches every child here

effects.log: {sac_name} considers it. 'That is true.'

events.text: You spend the lantern night beside {sac_name}, on a barge drifting down the canal with a plate of rice-cakes between you. {sac_He} watches the paper lamps drift past and never once mentions the gate. You learn what it looks like when a friend is trying very hard to enjoy something for the last time.

choices.text: Let the lamps speak for you

effects.log: You float one with {sac_name}'s name on it. It sinks too soon.

choices.text: Ask what {sac_he} wants from the rest of the years

effects.log: 'Nothing hard,' says {sac_name}. 'Tea. Company. A boat.'

events.text: {sac_name} wants to see the harvest-moon from the top of the tallest hill, where the sky is closest. You carry two cushions and a flask up the footpath. At the top {sac_he} lies back in the grass and says the sky looks different when you know there is no more of it. It looks exactly the same. You both say it does not.

choices.text: Lie back beside {sac_him}

effects.log: The moon takes a long time to cross.

choices.text: Say the sky has waited this long

effects.log: 'So can I,' says {sac_name}. It is not a promise.

events.text: It is done. The breath you carried for thirty years ran out of you and into {sac_name} through the cup of your joined hands, a single warm thread, and you felt yourself becoming plainer and quieter. {sac_name} opens {sac_his} eyes on a sky that has never looked so high. 'I can feel it,' {sac_he} whispers. 'The lid. It has lifted.'

choices.text: Stay beside {sac_him} while it settles

effects.log: The first night of {sac_realm} is the best night either of you can remember.

effects.log: 'Whose home?' asks the child. 'Mine,' you say, and are surprised to mean it.

You hear a child calling to the bell, in a low sing-song, as if it were a friend. It is {wo7_name}, high in the broken stair, who has been feeding the bell crusts of bread. The bell, of course, has not eaten.

She looks at {wo7_name} in your arms, then at your coat, then at the long grey river, and says: 'The ferry has a loft. Children like lofts. Nobody counts the hay.'

The ferry-woman says the god of this reach is a modest sort and does not mind bread. She adds, with a straight face, that river gods are known to look kindly on children who have lost things.

effects.log: A coin. A prayer. The river runs a little clearer.

Mother?' You say your own. The clerk looks at {wo7_name}'s accent and writes down nothing. The pen hovers.

events.text: The king's court keeps captive children in a pretty courtyard called the Orchard, where they are taught the court's letters and its hymns. {wo7_name} has a bench under a plum tree, a slate and a daily portion of rice. The master of the Orchard says the child is a credit. You are allowed to visit on the first of each month, with a clerk.

events.text: The court wants the other kingdom to know their child is safe in royal hands. A letter is drawn up, signed by the chancellor, and sent with a drummer. You are asked to add your name as a witness. The letter is gracious. The letter is also a rope with a ribbon tied on it.

effects.log: The chancellor notes it. Nobody argues. Everybody remembers.

events.text: A white cloth on a long pole is a very small thing, and you carry it up the river road toward the other kingdom's border with a child holding your free hand. At the ford two pickets watch from the far bank, one with a crossbow. {wo7_name} begins, unprompted, to whistle the lullaby. After four notes, the crossbow is lowered.

effects.log: The tune carries over the water. The whole bank goes quiet.

events.text: A carter brings a rumour of a chandler at a southern port who sells lamps with a tin whistle stamped on each base, and gives free oil to any child who asks. You buy a lamp from the next peddler who comes through, stamped the same. It burns steadily and smells faintly of the river.

effects.log: The reply is a lamp-wick. It is enough.

The ferry-woman breaks a bottle of rice-wine on her bow, and {wo7_name} reads out the name to the crowd on the bank. They do not know the story, but they cheer anyway. You stand in the crowd with your heart in your throat.

events.text: A court notice is nailed to the post at the ferry-landing: the king's wards of the river districts are to be given offices, and {wo7_name}, once a ward of the Orchard, is the new assessor of tolls. The notice does not mention you. The first toll collected on your ferry-run, a month later, is waived by a stamp, in a hand you know from a slate long ago.

Someone you do not know presses a bowl of river-snail soup into your hands and bursts into tears. You eat it, slowly. It is the best you have ever tasted, and you have no idea why that makes you weep too.

The tax roll lists the ferry as run by two persons, and so it is. Each spring you cross at dawn and say good morning to the girl at the stern, whoever she is.

effects.log: The reply is the same.

choices.text: Leave a small gift in the landing's bowl

effects.log: The river god takes the credit.

events.text: In the kitchen of a house you have only just entered, the cook hums a lullaby over the stove, a plain tune from the other side of a border. You have never heard it. Your throat closes anyway. The cook looks at you kindly. 'Everyone says that,' the cook says. 'Sit down. There's soup.' You sit. The soup is salty and perfect.

choices.text: Ask what the tune is called

effects.log: 'The Ferry Song,' says the cook, 'or the one we sing to children who are lost.'

choices.text: Hum the second verse

effects.log: You know it. The cook drops the ladle.

events.text: A boy of about seven on the bank of a river you are crossing waves at you, wide and hopeful, and shouts: 'Are you the one who found me?' The ferryman laughs and says the boy asks it of every passenger. You wave back anyway, and your chest aches, and the boat bumps the far landing.

choices.text: Wave until the boy is out of sight

effects.log: The ache fades. The warmth does not.

choices.text: Ask the ferryman about the boy

effects.log: 'An orphan,' says the ferryman. 'There are a few.'
